title: Passkeys and the post-password world
body_md:
## Understand the key and the remaining doors

A passkey is a WebAuthn credential for a particular service, based on a public and private key. At registration the service stores a public key; at sign-in an authenticator uses the private key to answer a fresh challenge. The private key is not typed into the page. The credential is tied to the service identifier, so a lookalike site cannot obtain a valid sign-in response for the real service when WebAuthn is implemented correctly. This protects the authentication exchange, not every action you might take after login.

The word “passkey” does not guarantee one storage model. Some credentials remain on a physical key or one device; others sync through a platform or credential manager. The provider controls how the synced copy is protected and recovered. Your face or fingerprint usually unlocks the local authenticator; the site receives proof of authentication, not your biometric image. A device PIN can also unlock it, so a weak device lock or shared device matters. Some deployments use a passkey for passwordless sign-in, while others use it as an additional factor. Check what the specific service actually does.

### Registration and cross-device use

Create a passkey only while signed in through the service's independently opened settings and only on a device you control. Name or identify the device if the service permits, then test a fresh sign-in. A phone can sometimes approve sign-in on another computer through a QR-based cross-device flow; this is not the same as copying the key into that computer. If a passkey prompt appears unexpectedly, cancel it and open the service yourself. A QR code is a route into a protocol, not proof that the surrounding page is trustworthy.

### Lockout and fallback

List where each passkey lives, whether it syncs, and what happens if that device or its sync account is unavailable. Protect the sync account and device; keep a supported backup method. If you lose a device, revoke its passkey or session in the real service and follow the platform's device-loss procedure. Do not assume every passkey becomes inaccessible when one platform account is lost: a separate hardware key or another synced provider may remain. Conversely, a passkey does not necessarily remove an old password, SMS recovery or a help-desk reset path. Review those paths as part of the upgrade.

widget_config.goal: Enroll and test a passkey while identifying its storage, device-risk and account-recovery paths.
widget_config.today_action: For one service that offers passkeys, read its own sign-in settings, create a passkey on a personal device, test sign-in, and record the supported backup and removal path.
widget_config.scope: General WebAuthn explanation; Google procedures are Google-account-specific. Storage, sync and fallback vary by service and provider. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: Passkey offered on a borrowed laptop
blocks.situation: A synthetic travel site shows “Create a passkey” while you are signed in on a library computer. The browser suggests saving it on this computer.
blocks.analysis: Do not register a credential on a device you do not control. Use your own phone through a supported cross-device flow or wait for your own device; sign out of the borrowed machine.

blocks.title: A legitimate cross-device QR prompt
blocks.situation: A synthetic account opened from your own bookmark offers a QR prompt on your laptop so your nearby phone can approve login. You initiated the sign-in and the account page is verified.
blocks.analysis: This may be a legitimate WebAuthn cross-device flow. Confirm the initiating page and phone prompt, then approve on your phone. The QR itself is not the trust anchor; your independently opened service and expected action are.

blocks.title: Add a passkey without losing access
blocks.setup: Synthetic learning-platform account supports passkeys, still allows a password, and lists devices in security settings.

choices.text: Open the platform independently, sign in and use its account security settings.
choices.consequence: The passkey is created for the intended service.
choices.explanation: An invitation link is unnecessary for sensitive enrollment.

choices.text: Scan a passkey setup QR from an unsolicited message.
choices.consequence: An unknown page can start a different flow.
choices.explanation: A QR code does not certify the service behind it.

steps.prompt: The browser asks where to save the passkey. What matters?

choices.text: Choose a personal authenticator and note whether it syncs or stays device-bound.
choices.consequence: You know which account or device must survive for later sign-in.
choices.explanation: Passkey storage and backup are provider-dependent.

choices.text: Choose a shared family laptop because it is nearby.
choices.consequence: Other people who unlock it may be able to sign in.
choices.explanation: Passkeys should be registered only on controlled devices.

steps.prompt: The new passkey works. What is the next security check?

choices.text: Inspect existing password, MFA and recovery methods still accepted by the service.
choices.consequence: You see the remaining access paths.
choices.explanation: A passkey enrollment does not automatically close older routes.

choices.text: Assume the service disabled its password and SMS recovery.
choices.explanation: Check the actual settings rather than assuming migration is complete.

steps.prompt: Your phone with the passkey is lost. What now?

choices.text: Use a supported backup to enter the verified service, revoke the lost device’s credential and review sessions.
choices.consequence: The lost credential is addressed without trusting a stranger’s link.
choices.explanation: Revocation and device controls are service-specific; a backup plan makes them reachable.

choices.text: Wait: biometrics make a lost phone impossible to misuse.
choices.explanation: A device may be unlocked by PIN, and loss also creates lockout risk.

blocks.debrief: Passkeys protect a particular authentication exchange. Safe use still includes device ownership, fallback inventory and loss response. Retry any uncertain decision.

questions.prompt: What does a correctly implemented passkey stop?

choices.text: A lookalike origin obtaining a valid authentication response for the real service.
choices.explanation: WebAuthn binds the credential to the service identifier.

choices.text: Every scam after the account is open.
choices.explanation: A passkey does not judge payments, messages or actions after login.

choices.text: No; it can be synced or device-bound depending on the authenticator.
Yes; all passkeys live in one platform cloud.
choices.explanation: Physical and device-bound credentials also exist.

questions.prompt: After adding a passkey, what should you verify?

choices.text: The old password and recovery routes the service still accepts.

choices.explanation: Local unlock is one part of the account’s access design.
